THE COMPLETE CYCLE

One connector, start to finish.

Choose a case. Scrub any step. Inspect the connector up close.

In the simulation today

Rigid plug/socket contact, retract-and-search, an ideal latch and a depth-based continuity check with injected faults. The complete cycle above is a scripted illustration. Open the experiment below for computed contact forces.

The first physical cell adds

Operator loading, the nest and cable comb, vision registration, grasp checks, real force sensing, a wired tester, release and per-unit records. The turnover cradle adds a supported regrasp before insertion. A new part needs quick-change fingers, a nest insert, a board plate and taught targets, plus depth, press and pull limits from its datasheet and a pinout.

Still to be proven

False passes remain an open problem: a half-seat can read continuous, and friction can make a pull pass. Still unproven: latch and pin damage at seating force, cable loads that tilt the housing, board flex that changes the force reading, cycle time against a skilled person, and a safety assessment for working near people.

Saved offsets belong to the fixture and are checked on every part: calibration, not learning. Two passing checks out of three is a fail. Any failed check stops the unit; retry once, then extract under a force limit, reject and retain the trace for a person to clear the fault.

    INTERACTIVE SOFTWARE PROTOTYPE

    Inside the simulation.

    A tool pushes a connector into a socket. MuJoCo works out the motion and forces in your browser.

    The search
    If the plug hits, it backs off and tries a little to each side. When one spot works, it keeps it. It never sees where the socket is. This is a fixed search, not a learned skill.
    The checks
    Connected means the plug went in deep enough. Locked means it held when pulled. You can force either to fail. There is no real wiring or latch.
    The limits
    Sizes and forces are made up. Only the plug and socket touch; everything else is for show. The full-cycle view illustrates the camera, cable handling and operator workflow. Those systems are not physically simulated. The contact experiment resets by extracting the same plug; the full-cycle illustration leaves an accepted plug seated.
    Next
    Build the real robot and run it on customer parts. This page shows the idea, not how it does in a factory.
